opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the commitment to open-endedness makes me fundamentally optimistic, but in a slightly different way than people usually mean when they talk about progress in AI.

A lot of the current discourse treats progress as climbing a fixed hill: you pick a benchmark, you scale up data and compute, and you watch the number go up. That has worked remarkably well, and I don't want to downplay it. But from an open-endedness perspective, the more interesting question isn't how high we can climb on a given hill. It's whether our systems can discover new hills, generate their own problems, and accumulate stepping stones that weren't obvious in advance. If you look at natural evolution or at the history of science, the big leaps rarely came from optimizing a predefined objective. They came from exploring, from collecting interesting artifacts that later turned out to be crucial for something else entirely.

So when I ask how much room there is for further progress, my answer is: an enormous amount, because we've mostly been operating in a closed-world setting. We train models on a static snapshot of human data and evaluate them on tasks we've already defined. The moment you close the loop, so that systems generate hypotheses, run experiments, evaluate the results, and feed those back into their own learning, you move into a regime where the space of what can be discovered keeps expanding rather than saturating.

That's a big part of why I've been excited about things like automating parts of the scientific process and about meta-learning more broadly, using learning systems to discover better learning algorithms, optimizers, or objectives themselves. It's a very practical way of saying: let's not hand-design everything; let's let the search process find things we wouldn't have thought of.

I should also be honest about the hard problems. Open-ended systems need a notion of what's interesting, and that's really difficult to formalize. Novelty alone isn't enough; you can generate infinite noise that's technically novel. Foundation models help here, because they carry a lot of human intuition about what's interesting or worthwhile, but they also inherit our biases and might just keep us near the existing distribution. Then there's evaluation: as systems produce more of their own artifacts, verifying that those artifacts are actually correct and valuable becomes a bottleneck. And of course there are real safety considerations once systems start setting their own goals.

But to me those are research problems, not ceilings. Open-endedness tells me the ceiling isn't really set by the size of the internet or by any single benchmark. It's set by how well we can build systems that keep generating their own curriculum and keep surprising us. And I think we're only at the very beginning of that.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think my commitment to open-endedness makes me fundamentally optimistic about how much room there is, but it also changes what I think "progress" even means.

If you look at the way most of the field measures progress right now, it's benchmark-driven. We define a target, we optimize toward it, we saturate it, and then we go find a new target. And that's been incredibly productive, I don't want to dismiss it. But it's a closed-ended view of progress. The ceiling is defined in advance by whoever wrote the benchmark. Every time we pick an objective, we're implicitly saying "this is what intelligence looks like," and then we get something that's very good at exactly that and often surprisingly brittle just outside it.

Open-endedness, as I think about it, coming from work like Ken Stanley's and Jeff Clune's, and what we've been trying to do at Sakana with things like the AI Scientist, flips that around. The question isn't "how do we hit the target," it's "how do we build systems that keep generating their own novel and learnable targets." Novelty and learnability together. A system that produces things that are new to an observer but still comprehensible and buildable-upon. That's the engine behind biological evolution, behind human culture, behind science itself. None of those processes had a fixed objective, and yet they produced the most complex artifacts we know of.

So when people ask "are we hitting a wall," I think they're usually asking about the closed-ended regime. Will scaling pretraining keep paying off, will the data run out. Those are real questions. But from an open-ended perspective they're almost beside the point, because the real source of further progress isn't more of the same data, it's getting systems into a loop where they generate their own experience, their own problems, their own evaluation signals, and where the hard part is deciding what's interesting rather than just getting better at a known task.

And honestly, that reframing makes me think we're very early. We've gotten extremely good at compression and interpolation over the human record. We've barely started on the question of how a system decides what to explore next, how it maintains diversity instead of collapsing onto a few solutions, how it builds a stepping stone that only makes sense in hindsight. Those are the mechanisms that produced everything interesting in nature, and we have very rudimentary versions of them in AI. So the room for progress, to me, isn't a few more points on a leaderboard. It's an entire dimension we've mostly been ignoring.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes me quite reluctant to say that we’re close to the end of progress, because open-endedness is really about the possibility of continually discovering things that you couldn’t specify in advance. You can solve a benchmark, but that doesn’t mean you’ve exhausted the space of interesting problems—or even found the right problems to work on.

For me, the exciting question is whether we can build systems that keep generating new challenges and developing the capabilities to meet them. There’s a feedback loop there: new capabilities make new problems accessible, and those problems create pressure for further learning. Evolution is an inspiration for thinking about that, although reproducing that kind of process computationally is far from straightforward.

So I see a lot of room for progress. But I wouldn’t equate open-endedness with simply making today’s models bigger. It also asks us to think about environments, interactions, and how a system discovers what to learn next. How do you get sustained, meaningful novelty rather than just endless variation? I think that’s a very rich direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes me quite optimistic, because open-endedness asks a slightly different question. Instead of asking, “How well can we solve this particular benchmark?” you ask, “Can we build a process that keeps discovering new problems and developing the capabilities needed to solve them?” And those are very different ambitions.

Evolution is a useful example here. You have this relatively simple underlying process, but the environments and the interactions between organisms generate an enormous diversity of strategies. The challenge for AI is understanding which ingredients allow that continual production of novelty, rather than a system converging on one solution and stopping.

So I see a lot of room for progress in how we construct learning environments, how agents generate their own challenges, and how we retain and build on discoveries. Scaling models can contribute to that, but there’s also a question about the process around the model: what drives exploration, what makes a discovery useful, and how does it create opportunities for further discoveries?

I wouldn’t claim that open-ended progress happens automatically. Producing something different is much easier than producing something that opens up a meaningful new direction. But that gap is precisely why I think there’s so much interesting work left to do.
